blocks.x: Do that with a pencil and paper though. That's before things happen. Yeah, I remember Robert years back. I just met him once in a bar, you know, but he seemed to...
He always wear tansy during an hour and store at me. Really, yeah?
Let's see if it seems to be picking us up.
He's a gal.
Oh, yeah.
He's all a rich old lady's friend. Oh, really? He was a smart man, wasn't he? He had something figured out. Well, I'm just talking, you know, don't quote me.
You on tape now? Yeah. Let's have you say your name, Buzzy. Your real name.
Byers, B-Y-E-R-S is my first name. I only have one name, Byers Williams. But everyone calls you Buzzy. Yeah.
His nickname is Buzzy. Where'd you pick up the nickname?
How long ago?
Well, they're buzzing on the piano.
Oh, really? Yeah.
You want me to say a little about how I happened to come down to where my mother and father
was? Well, let's get everybody's name down so we'll know who's talking. All right. See if it works, okay? Kurt?
I'm Kurt Gerdy.
You hear from the archive along with Dick Allen.
And yours? Mine is Tony Felici. B-I-L-E-C-I. And I'm Dick Allen. And we all seem to be picking up. So, you can start with the beginning of your life if you want to.

I tell it to start from when you come down here. Is that what you want? Well, I'd like to know how old he is, too. Well, tell them how old you are. You all right? I'm going on 90. I'm going on 90. I'm going on 90. I'm going on 90. That's right. Listen, my mother and father, my father was a concert singer.
He sang with Mary Gardner and other singers. He sang also with a Philadelphia Philharmonic orchestra. My mother was a fine pianist. And they sang before the King and Queens in Crystal Palace, London.
My goodness.

I was born a scared kid. My older sister used to pick up with a buggy, a boogeyman. I was so frightened I'd go to school. This is a true story. Byers watched two and two. Bingo. It's gone, see. I really went to the fifth grade. And I got so damn nervous. I told my father I want to go to work. Well, around 1919, they had avatars working at the 112th Street in Amsterdam, Avenue across the street from St. John's Cathedral. It's the second largest in the world. And all it had was one arch. It would take all day to get one of those big blocks up there. But they used to advertise streetcar rides to Philadelphia for a dollar and ten cents. That's right. It goes to Newark, Elizabeth, Trenton, and then to Philadelphia. So I left home. I'm telling the truth. I didn't tell my father nothing. Because I wanted to go out for myself. When I got to Philadelphia, I walked to Chester. And on come of Baltimore and Ohio railroad train. You go for two cents a mile them days. And I went to Baltimore. And I walked out towards Sparrow Point. And I heard the piano. And I was drinking Sash Brutal. So I went to the bar. A fellow named Sylvester Williams was playing. I said, I play. He got me a job next, that night. For one dollar. So that dollar, well, I had a couple dollars. So I took a streetcar ride. And the freight train blocks the train. So the train just dragged. And so I jumped out and climbed on them. And I went to Hagerstown. Hagerstown, I took another train and wound up in Louisville, Kentucky. I took another train and wound up, I don't know, something just told me, go. And I went to Jackson, Tennessee. And there's a moving picture where the train stopped. I went there. He said, I couldn't afford to pay a dollar a night. It was called Nicolette's, Nicololium's, Nic-5 cents for it, see. Got to have 20 people in there to make a buck. He says, where do you want to go? I said, I want to go to New Orleans. So he called a fellow outside. He says, here's the fellow who wants to go to New Orleans. He was a messenger. They had a car on it waiting to be picked up there. We're half a load of chickens and then half the car were eggs. The fellow took, let me go. So when he got to Jackson, he got to Carlton Avenue, he says, it's a good place to go to New Orleans. So instead of me not knowing the town, I walked all around the riverfront to Parker Street. Well, I had no place to go and I was kind of afraid. So I slept under a tarpaulin. They only had one shed then days. That's back in 1910 now. About about 1909. One shed on the, that was the Parker Street. So I got up in the morning, washed, I started walking. First thing I know, I was in Storyville. So I thought it was one of his, Alice, his Jenny on the doors and all that, the cribs and stuff, see. And there's a fellow, my name is George Spaffer, used to fix all the electricity for the cribs and everything else. And he's fixing with the piano. They had them days of things, the contraction turned down and had all the tin things on, and it sounded like a mandolin with the piano, see. So I got told him, he said, go around the corner of Pop Towers, Basin, Bienville Street. That's where the piano players used to hang out, they played for Little White, Josie Arlington, Dixie Shaver. So I met Mila Kuhn, they called him Stale Bread. So we started, he called it Buskin, so we used to go into Cadillac, Black Cat, San Suzie. They were different places, they had a piano. I played a little piano, he'd sing a song, I played a little piano. He'd sing a song and he'd pass the trade. We'd make fifteen, twenty, twenty-five cents. Now he got me a room at 708 Royal Street. They advertised, I'd see pictures doing carnival, with this fancy grill boy up the- The Okinaikon.
Yeah.

Yeah. Yeah, I know that. A dollar and a half, a dollar and a half a week. Yeah. He introduced me to red beans and rice at the Chinamans for a nickel. I swear. China's eating in the world. And they sold, they sold two, two pork chops for a dime. Well, they used to go in Martins, in the alley, and have a big piece of roast beef there. They'd give you one slice of bread cutting and put that roast beef on it. And they had free lunch, free lunch, a bunch of cheese and stuff and stuff. And there comes along a fellow with a big hamper, biggest hamper ever seen, full of shrimp. Ten for a nickel. Ten for a nickel. I mean big ones. Yeah. Nickel. That's true. Well, I stayed around, oh yes, I wasn't there long when my father's friend, Mr. Gibson, who was the stage manager for Talk on the York Show, one of the George N. Cohen Show. I was living at the Bush Hotel with another piano player named Kid Ross for seven dollars a week. Later he was called a senator. There were nice rooms. The fellow says, hey, bars, this is Mr. Gibson, so why don't you go home? So I went home, I told my father I wanted to go for my soap. So I finally went out with a sign painter out of New York City, painting all that I do is the fellow around that was black, see. They had a regular painter with him, see. There was three in one oil, two of the advertisements, I forget the other ones, see. And we got to Scranton, Pennsylvania. He liked to sing this, my boss that I worked for, see. He had a loud, loud voice, like, hey, the foot of stars are shining, all that kind of stuff. So the fellow was sitting at the piano, happened to be the owner of this Conway Hotel, they call it the Conway House, that's just called the smaller places around Scranton. And he says, you want a job? I said, I don't play for a living. I'll give you fifteen dollars a week and borrow the larger. The coal miners were making fifteen dollars a week, that's all they were making. I mean, hard coal, anthracite coal. So I got, so I'm going back to New Orleans, I couldn't say where. I made three trips back in fourth New Orleans. And the last trip, I was in Omaha playing for Gus Wick, whose wife was a lady in blue at the, at the, at the, uh. Blue Rose? Yeah. See. Well, I stayed at his house about three weeks, they opened the place, you know. And, uh, that's where I met Mamie Lee Kelly. Mamie Lee Kelly, I went and worked for her two nights, she never paid me.
When Gus Wick opened up, we had a makeup box.
Ben Bard, who married Ruth Holland, and, uh, Martha Pryor, beautiful boxing girl, saying, I ain't got no body, don't shake my tree. Pieces, something like that.
I get the idea.

And I worked, I worked, I played for her at the Dauphine Theater, and I forgot the name of the piano player. He was violin there for years, he was playing the show. So he sat out there and watched me, cause she was singing, instead of easy keys, instead of F, it'd be four sharps. Instead of being flat, it'd be five sharps. And I can, listen, I only had five lessons. I worked with Johnny Krueger at the, at the Colleton Sisters for eight months, and I was going crazy cause I'd take some of the heavy stuff. I, I used to, I don't know, my mother was a fine pianist, my father, like I told her, sang her. They sang the Academy of Music in New York and all that.
Yeah. I couldn't take any lessons.

I couldn't take any lessons. I'm pretty sure I didn't have no more than five or six. But I could go out and pick up Rosier Grady, take East Side, West Side, from a little number that taught me from the company. And I finally jumped around the piano and went down the bass and later on I found augments and diminishes and all that kind of stuff. It come to me natural. See? Well I go back to Mila Coma again, twice. I couldn't stay away with rice and beans and good gumbo and good fine oysters that fifteen cents a dozen, two dozen for a quarter, a big glass of beer, you know, for nickel. Well we never had those things up in New York. I'm born in Louisville, Kentucky, see. My father took us all as kids to New York, my mother, and they went and sing an opera, so. But anyway that's how I got to New Orleans. I took freight trains and what they call side dog Pullmans. Yeah. What year did you get here?
What year did you get here first? 1910.

1910. That's seventy years ago. I'll be ninety next April. And this is what's kept me alive, I tell everybody drink beer. Well New York's at Egan telling me when we worked at the nightclub, I used to drink six and seven. Just cause the people bought them.
That's why they called me a play bar, cause I used to drink beer with you. Did you know Irving Leclair?
Know who? Irving Leclair?
Yeah, Irving Leclair was a nice piano player. That was a guy who played a couple of keys, key of D. He wrote triangle jazz. Sure I remember. Sure I remember. Leclair?
Oh, it was Leclair? Yeah. He was a singer, wasn't he? Piano, pianist.
Piano player. Piano player. He sang too, didn't he? He and Eddie McCarthy had a band. Eddie McCarthy.
Well that's right, but he was playing piano.
He wrote triangle blues and he wrote tropical girl. Yeah. You heard it? Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah, and then...
He heard it Saturday, huh?
Uh-huh. Well he wrote that. Yeah. And he wrote another fine number. I forgot it's a beautiful thing.
Sure.

Well I was with Tommy Lyman in New York for seven years and a couple months, and a couple of those songs, when he found out I knew those songs he used and was crazy about them. Well how am I doing? Fine. I'm great.
Erwin Leclair has moved out to Jefferson Parish now. No, Orvin's not living.
Erwin Leclair? Yes he is.
Last time I talked to him he was alive. Well I'll be damned. Tell him hello for me.
I will.
But he's getting very forgetful. Yeah. Oh yes. But you know, he has good moments and bad moments.
Last time I seen Orvin was waiting for the electric company here.
Yeah, his daughter plays piano now. She does, yeah.
Well somebody told me he had died. I thought...

No, not that I've heard of and I keep in touch with him and I see him, because there's a band here that plays my wonderful Tropical Girl and Triangle Jazz Blues. Beautiful though. And they had a recording session, he went to it on Saturday, I didn't make it.
The New Leviathan, the original? No, the New Leviathan. New Leviathan.
The Oriental Foxtrot Orchestra. And they do all those numbers like Dardanella and as well as a lot of the local numbers. They do Purple, Rosa, Cairo sometimes.
Well maybe Lee Kelly come into the Court of Two Sisters when Tony and I was working in the courtyard place, I don't know what they... What was it called?
Huh? That room we were in. Jimmy Cooper built that little place in the back. You're talking about the place on Bourbon? Yeah.
The Court Tavern. The Court Tavern, that's right.

Yeah, that's right. He built a tavern for me and him. Yeah. That's right. He built a piano, what they call a gay nineties in there. Uh-huh. Him and I was raised, we had blazers and I had a straw hat and I raised a mustache. We had another fellow working behind a boy named Bobby Lay, who was an old entertainer from around California. And we had a bartender to sing by the name of Jimmy. Jimmy. He had a big flat place in the back. He had a big flat place in the back. He had a big flat place in the back. He had a big flat place in the back. He had a big flat place in the back. See, Jimmy Cooper told me, says, if you quit going to New York, play for Tommy Lyman, I'll fix that room up. See? Well, maybe Lee Kelly comes in there. There's one song I never did forget, I had to write me the voice out.

She paints her cheeks like roses She paints her way dear smile She colours up She paints them black or brown. She paints her lips rosy red, puts on a silken gown, and every night you'll find her painting New Yorktown. You see, after 1915, people used to frown on people using paint. I remember when I first came here, I could still see them. People would be sitting on the front porch and taking red brick, shacking it down. I'm talking about people in town.
Sure. And painting. Really?
Yeah. So she didn't like that very much.

We used to use red brick. We had to wash the steps on a Saturday morning. In them days, when we was kids, you had to wash the front steps, you know. You always kept them nice and clean. And then after we washed them, we'd grind this brick up fine and throw it all over those steps. Well, some people did it to keep the bumps from sitting on these steps, you know. Dirty them up. But that was our job when we was kids. Every Saturday we had to go out and clean them and wash the back and wash the front steps. And we always had to do something. And if you were a real good kid, they'd give you a big nickel, you know.

Nickel was a big thing in them days. Yeah. Well, listen, the only thing I can tell you about, when I, I'll use the expression bumming for the meal, stale bread. Why, we used to go around and listen to Tony Jackson.
Oh, really?
Yeah. He was waiting for Gypsy Shafer. So on our way back, the second street, the next street behind Basin used to be called Franklin. They've changed it now, I understand.
Franklin's right. Yeah.

Crozat is what it's called now, but that's, it used to be Franklin. So we got, we walked back, I met Tony Perini, but I didn't know him that day. Yeah. He used to come around and listen to him. And Tony Jackson played a marvelous piano, he could sing like a woman. And when I was at Omaha, he wrote Pretty Baby, when I was at Omaha I picked up a copy of music of Some Sweet Day, had to go to color shows. See up in New York, people that had to go to color shows, they couldn't go to white. Beautiful number. Some sweet day I'm going to find somebody. And I want to get things right. Yeah, so we left, we left, we sat outside of Gypsy Shafer and listened to him play. So we got to Franklin, Basin, Pop Torres on Basin in Bienville. Across the way from the Broadway, of course Lil Weiss was next door. Buddy Ford, the detective got killed in the Broadway, you see. But I'm getting away from my story, I want to finish. When we got to the corner of Franklin and Bienville, we seen a fellow run out from across the street, who was called the White Rock Saloon. He had a gun in his hand. It seemed like at the 101 hand, Tuxedo sent the dip of blood, come down. I grabbed me and I said, come on, those small blocks, so we went down and popped over. I laid down and we heard the shooting. I don't know which one of the Parker boys, it was Frank and Harry. And the guy run the Tuxedo, he was killed. So that's that one.
That was a very sensational case in those days. Oh yeah, they closed everything down, I've heard.

My teacher was working that night, I had a music teacher who worked on Franklin Street. They called him Hoss, I don't know if you remember him, he's from across the river. Fess they called him, you know, Professor Mineta. Oh yes, yes. Yeah, and he and Peter Bocards were telling me about it.

Well, I'll tell you about Sidney Bourgeois, you read about the killing and all like that? Mm-hmm. Sidney Bourgeois used to come into Pop Toros, that's based on Bambler Street, where the piano players, well there's only a few of them, one played for Lilla White and one for Josie Arlington. Of course, Tony Jackson never come in there, see. Well, me and I used to hang out there. Pop Toros used to use us quite often, see. He got a dollar and I got two dollars a night, see. So I used to walk a meal home. He lived off Broad Street, and the next block back he had a home back there. And I walked back. I was standing at the Bush Hotel. So I passed, it was called the Budweiser, but it used to be like the Pup, the Pup was a beer hall. You know, I had a piano player and girls were sitting around there, just like the Hundred and One Ranch. And I barely passed there and Mamie Lee Kelly, I heard Mamie Lee Kelly, she was bumming Sidney Bourgeois. And he had a gun in his hands. A year before that, sometime before that, and I always say it's a year, he had picked up a policeman and threw him in a bread case across the street where there was a restaurant. Well, the police had it in for Sidney Bourgeois. So I passed there, I said, uh-uh. This party got across the street and heard the shots. Sidney Bourgeois was killed, see.
Did you tell him who? I'm telling the truth. Did you tell him who Sidney Bourgeois is? Who, if he knew who Sidney Bourgeois was?
No. No, I never did know him. Sidney Bourgeois was a professor.

He was a mathematician in the Spencer College. Oh. We had a pop tour, he'd come in, put your figures down, nines and eights and sevens and mix them all up. Very smart man. Boom, boom, boom, boom. Right to answer. But when he was in, he was in pop tours one day, he was a well, a good dresser, Sidney Bourgeois. And the gentleman with him had nice clothes on. All at once, boom, he hit his friend. For what?

Sidney Bourgeois hit his friend? Oh, he was a terrific puncher. When he was a professor, when he got to drinking, he was a tough man. He was really tough. And if he hit you one time, he was going. He was a tough puncher. Take two, three men to take care of him, the guy he's tough.
So, Stadbury and I sat on that, far from it, and Stadbury walks over to Sidney, and said, don't you ever hit me. Stadbury can fight. I got a group of friends.
You know something? Maybe you might not be mentioning names because they might sue you. You might have some relatives living here.
I don't think they can do that. Huh? They can.
I mean, he's been dead a while. Well, that's an old faculty telling me. Yeah.

Well, that's about all the roughness I know around there, because they had the pimps and all that around there, you know. But they didn't hang out with Frank Torres. See, Frank Torres would invite the show from the Burlesque, Rose, who ran the, who was that running, Ryan? Huh? What's that, is that, was the Burlesque, what's that? Dolphin Theatre. Huh? Dolphin Theatre. Dolphin Theatre. Yeah. Blue Rose run it, see. Mm-hm. And I was up in Birmingham working for Gus Wick. He had married this girl in blue that had been with the show. Gypsy Rose Lee she was, wasn't it? No. No, this woman's different. I don't know. And, well, I came down, I got married, and Emile introduced me to my wife. And I was married 50 years to her. Mm-hm. I went up to Birmingham to assist her, who I'm living with now, to celebrate. And I, they started, in Tuscaloosa, my nephew, that I raised, he was born in, in New York, and he was born in, in 1950. He's left five children. He passed away not long ago, see. And, uh, I left in Tuscaloosa, and I came back to New Orleans, and I was working at the, as a bank guard, at the Whitney Bank, and my nephew, my brother-in-law come in and says, Sessa called her, Sessa, my wife, and she's bad off. And I got up there, and she was in a coma, and she was dead next day, so I don't know. That's terrible. But Mamie Lee Kelly never liked me, I don't know why. And I worked for her two nights, she never played me. What did you say that?
Was she from, from here? Well, Mamie didn't know.
No. She was from out of town. And I don't know where really, where she was from.
Mamie Lee Kelly, as he knows, originally came from Panama. She didn't come from Panama. She didn't come from Panama.
She came from Omaha. Yeah, but she was a big shot in Panama. Well certainly, he's got the picture. She was on a big shot in Panama. Yeah, he's got the picture.
He's got the picture.
I gave him to Kurt to hold, because I was afraid I might spill beer on him.
Stale Bread played piano, did he? Who?

Well, he used to play Black Keys, you know. Black Keys. Okay, alright. And he claims he wrote the voice, he's a creator of jazz. That out, I got a paper about it, and on his grave he's got something about that. See, his daughter is married to Mr. Weaver. And I was out to the side, Tony came out, or Cindy rather, and went to the grave and put some flowers on it.
It's the first time I've seen him in thirteen years.

I stayed one time with Tony for thirteen months, second time eleven months. I was really here two years with him. We drank up here, and we used to talk. Tony was a good entertainer. I was. He used to sing risque songs. Nothing dirty, no fault of the words.
Well, every, it's that's what's called.
Who ate Nelly and the Belly of the Fish? What you call them? What was that?
I didn't get the name of it.
Who ate Nelly and the Belly, they called it the French Markets. Oh yeah.
Who ate Nelly and the Belly of the Fish? Oh yeah.
It's the mystery of the day. Who ate Nelly and the Belly of the Fish?
Well they had a lot of numbers around here years ago, if they claim was never, uh, risky. You might have heard one of them was hot nuts. You ever hear hot nuts? Hot peanuts. I've heard of it.
And Billy Price used to use that. I've heard of it.
Then he had another one called Nice Boy. That other? Nice Boy. He had a fellow like Billy Miller around here years ago, that featured sweet violets.

I don't know why I bless him, but I heard sweet violets. Yeah. I went to the club for 15 months. Billy Miller, yeah. The bass player? See I could, no he was the singer, comedian. Oh Billy. Comedian, yeah. Yeah.
Not Teddy Miller's brother. What? He's no kid to Teddy Miller.
You mean the little Miller you with no legs?
No legs, yeah. No, no. The kid with the no legs. He's daddy had a one man band. Yeah I used to see him by the fair and night.
Daddy used to play drums and everything at one time. And later on I played with Empty Daddy, little Teddy Miller. He had no legs.

And he used to come around and you know, push, what the hell you call it, I don't know. Tommy Harmon, who was with me. Oh man, he used to come around and tell them the clubs and you know, do a few numbers and they'd show him some tips. And I think he used to go in Royal and Canal and I was running. I was running. He comes down against me. I was with him sitting. We worked at the Piper Rock, two seasons. We had Martin Downey, Luther Guard. You know that guy, Lyman, he's talking about?
Tommy Lyman?

Yeah, but not much. Fair enough. We had four of them. We'd go back next season for the racing season. And we had Sophie Tuggett, Joey Lewis, and Connie Boswell. Now you know he must be a good entertainer to play those places. I was with him, oh I made some money with that guy. Boswell's sister. Huh? Boswell's sister. Yeah.
Well who was the, I think starting him out was Bill Coker. Did you know Bill Coker?
No, I don't know him.

Well he was a famous newspaper man, either a sports writer or something, but he was originator of, I mean he got the Boswell's sister started I think, I don't know. Connie and the, what was it, two sisters? Connie was the crippled one. The crippled one, yeah.
Well Vett is still living, huh? No, they're all gone, no they're gone. One of them, one of them is alive. Yeah, there's a guy, there's a guy in Metry that keeps rights to all the time.
They broke up, you know, Connie went by herself for one.
Oh I know, but he was asking about the other one being alive. I don't know who.
Yeah, that is the one that's alive. Now who wrote the Kansas City Torch? You know that, Tony?

Tommy Lyman wrote that, I have a copy of it. When the gang was all gone once around the town looking for friends and company. We know it. Oh, excuse me Tony. No, I said we know it. I didn't say nothing about you except we know it. I thought you were going to do a duet. Yeah, I just was thinking that, you know, I heard that song. He wrote that, he was a very good entertainer. Yeah.
And he was smart. I mean he let somebody make him remarks and he turned around and make him look that small.

He had all the answers. He was a top entertainer around the yard. Oh yes, he was marvelous. He was very superstitious. We were working at Leslie House. Now in New York you can't work seven days a week. And he went before the union and he raised so much care and they allowed him. We had to work seven. Why do you want to work seven days? For me. For me. For me.
For me.

For me. For me. For me. For me. For me. For me. For me. For me. For me. For me. For me. For me. For me. For me. Well, I got friends coming from Chicago, going to Paris, blah, blah, blah. So I'm the only guy in New York in them days who could work seven days. So we're working at Leslie House. It's called the Blair House now on West 56th Street. Unless they change the name again. Harry K. Thor, what's his name? Harry K. Thor.
Sanford White.

He built that building. And about the third night, I don't drink on the job. I'm telling the truth. He wouldn't stand for it. I never did the last one. But I had to go. I'm going around the steps and go do my business. And when I come back, he's coming down the stairs. So, boom!
You were talking about the rainy night there and you came in with umbrellas and all that, raincoats there, with Tommy Lyman. Go ahead. I got it. Well, in the morning it was time to go home,

when he see an umbrella, he jumped from here to that next room. He says, you bore the hell out of me. He says, my brothers went out, what do you call them? High-heft boots. High-button shoes. High-button shoes. And we were waking up at the piping rock, the porter comes along in the morning, sweeping along in the bar, see. He said, you let me get a drink then. You want a drink of this? Yeah, so. I drink beer. So I get a beer. And along comes the porter sweeping the floor with all the small brooms. And he sees that broom, he misjumped me across the street. That's how superstitious he was. Now listen, he wasn't too hard for me to play for. He liked me because I knew maybe 300 songs. And he did too, see. And Reese Haber-Herschel at the Brill Bill and that was Jack Tempsey's restaurant. And that's a building full of records, where they make records and stuff. And I had some fellas come in and listen to Tommy and I. So I wouldn't do that. I said, what do you mean? Tommy and I would start out, I was born in Virginia, but they'd go about 10 bars. And he raises his hand up, and I go from F to F sharp. And he says, in D wrote, uh, uh, there's a girl in the heart in Maryland. And that's in B flat, up his hand and puts me in five sharp. And he goes into Indy Road, Georgia, in my southern home, one of those things. And before I get through him playing five flats, the half a tone of key above C is five flats. And they go, and nothing could be fine in Sweetie Carolina in the morning. That's the kind of guy, no matter how I continue. We have a rehearsal, maybe twice a month, and he'd have three songs. You can't take no music on the job. Now that's, you got to have it there to learn all the numbers. See? Yeah. Oh, it was wonderful.
Who was Kid Ross?
Kid Ross was a piano player that, uh, well let me tell you how I come in town.
Uh-huh.

I left home and went to Philadelphia, bought a streetcar, went to Baltimore for two cents a mile on the Baltimore, Ohio. The fella gave me a job, and I got a buck that night, and I, uh, decided to take his streetcar, and the freight train is blocking us. He's just dragging. Now, what the hell made me in the mind to get out? And I got out and grabbed that train. And I went to, uh, uh, what do they call it, Maryland. And I took an elder named that had a branch on it into Louisville. Well, I'm born in Louisville. Uncle Sis and Aunt this.
Wait a minute. You done told that once before you're coming back.
Oh, wait a minute. I don't hear it. What do you say?
You told that once before you're coming back for the same thing you want to know about Kid Ross.
I'm going to tell him how I got to New Orleans.
You told him that before, didn't he?
Did I tell you about going to Jackson, Tennessee?
Yeah, you did.
You told him about that.
But you were going to tell us about Kid Ross.

Well, that's why I'm going to bring in Kid Ross. Yeah, okay. After I walked back in the district, and this fellow, George Spafford, was an electrician, took, you know, the cribs and all that, he sent me around Frank Torres. And Kid Ross was playing there, see? segments.title: Pre-interview chatter about a mutual acquaintance
segments.summary: Interviewer and Kurt Gerdy talk about a man they both knew while the recorder is tested.

segments.title: Names for the tape and how Byers became Buzzy
segments.summary: Williams gives his name, explains his nickname came from buzzing on the piano, and the people present introduce themselves.

segments.title: Parents: a concert-singer father and pianist mother
segments.summary: Williams, going on 90, says his father was a concert singer and his mother a fine pianist; they sang before royalty in London.

segments.title: Running away from home to New Orleans by freight train
segments.summary: Frightened and nervous at school, he leaves New York around 1909, plays a bar piano in Baltimore, rides trains to Jackson, Tennessee and then New Orleans, and ends up in Storyville meeting Stale Bread.

segments.title: Cheap eats, work in Scranton and Omaha, and Mamie Lee Kelly
segments.summary: Life in New Orleans with Stale Bread and Kid Ross, a stage manager's offer, a piano job in Scranton, and later work in Omaha where he played for Mamie Lee Kelly.

segments.title: Playing in difficult keys without lessons; arrival in 1910
segments.summary: He says he had only five or six lessons, learned by ear, kept returning to New Orleans, and first arrived there in 1910.

segments.title: Irving Leclair, his songs and the Oriental Foxtrot Orchestra
segments.summary: The group recalls pianist Irving Leclair, who wrote Triangle Jazz Blues and Tropical Girl, his health today and a band now playing his tunes.

segments.title: The Court Tavern with Tony and Jimmy Cooper
segments.summary: Williams and Tony worked in a gay-nineties tavern built for them behind the Court of Two Sisters on Bourbon Street.

segments.title: A song about painting, and red brick on the steps
segments.summary: He recalls a song about a woman who paints her cheeks and how people once frowned on paint; Gerdy remembers scouring steps with red brick.

segments.title: Tony Jackson, Gypsy Schaeffer's and the Tuxedo shooting
segments.summary: Walking with Stale Bread to hear Tony Jackson, Williams witnesses a gunman run out of the White Rock Saloon and the killing of the man who ran the Tuxedo.

segments.title: Sidney Bourgeois, the professor who was a tough fighter
segments.summary: Williams describes Pop Torres's place, Sidney Bourgeois the mathematician and puncher, and his death by shooting.

segments.title: Mamie Lee Kelly, Gus Wick and Williams's marriage
segments.summary: Further about Mamie Lee Kelly, who never paid him, where she came from, then his marriage, his wife's death and his job as a bank guard.

segments.title: Stale Bread, the black-key piano player
segments.summary: Williams says Stale Bread played the black keys, claimed to have created jazz, and has a grave he visited.

segments.title: Staying with Tony and the risque songs of the day
segments.summary: Williams recalls long stays with Tony and the risque novelty songs he sang, such as Who Ate Nelly and Hot Nuts.

segments.title: Billy Miller and little Teddy Miller
segments.summary: They sort out which Miller was meant: Billy Miller the singer-comedian, and Teddy Miller, the legless boy whose father played a one-man band.

segments.title: Two seasons at the Piping Rock with Tommy Lyman
segments.summary: Williams worked two seasons at the Piping Rock under Tommy Lyman, with headliners such as the Boswell Sisters, and notes Lyman wrote Kansas City Torch.

segments.title: Tommy Lyman's superstitions and working seven days at Leslie House
segments.summary: Lyman was a top entertainer, very superstitious, and got union permission for a seven-day week at Leslie House in New York.

segments.title: Lyman and the umbrella; his habit of calling keys
segments.summary: Lyman's fear of umbrellas and brooms, and how Williams followed his raised hand through key changes using about 300 songs.

segments.title: Retelling the trip to New Orleans before Kid Ross
segments.summary: Asked about Kid Ross, Williams starts over the freight-train journey until Gerdy reminds him he already told it.

segments.title: Kid Ross, Frank Torres's and playing at Josie Arlington's
segments.summary: Kid Ross, a black-key pianist, befriends him and sends him up to play at Josie Arlington's, where he is shocked by the naked dancing.

segments.title: Hippo, Billy's death and Tony's risque songs
segments.summary: After Billy died the risque songs fell to Tony; Williams discusses the catch lines and the worst song Tony sang.

segments.title: Williams's address and why he is called Buzzy
segments.summary: He gives his Birmingham address and explains that people in New Orleans and New York called him Buzzy instead of Byers.

segments.title: Tom Zimmerman and other names from the union magazine
segments.summary: The interviewer asks about various names; Williams recalls Tom Zimmerman, a heavy-drinking piano player at Tom Anderson's.

segments.title: Joe Martinez and the Dauphine Theatre police show
segments.summary: Joe Martinez the piano player, and the annual police show at the Dauphine with Buttercup Burns, for which Williams played without rehearsal.

segments.title: Kaz Art, Raymond Burke and family relations
segments.summary: Talk about whether Kaz Art was Peterson's or Raymond Burke's uncle, Burke's clarinet playing, and a story about his baby.
